author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Pin probe sample attribution under recursion

An ascription rebuilds its redex under its own id, and the evaluator's
delegation law is what stops that re-evaluation from opening a second
observation span. Nothing covered the law's stack-instance key: collapse
it so every call stack compares equal and the whole probe suite still
passes, while a ten-deep recursion silently reports one sample instead
of ten. These four pin one sample per call, two probes in one body
keeping separate sequences, one id sampled under two stacks, and mutual
recursion through a tuple binding.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Keep the collapsed ascription's id so its probe samples the value

Collapsing a pair of nested ascriptions minted the node with a fresh id,
so no evaluation ever ran under the inner ascription's id and the
evaluator could not open an observation span for it. The outermost
ascription of a chain was the only level that sampled at all; the others
sampled a value minted at collapse time, i.e. the operand unevaluated,
with the whole environment substituted into it.

Stamping the collapsed node with e's id -- what ID PRESERVATION FOR
PROBES at the top of this file already prescribes -- gives every level a
span that closes on the final value, so the collapse-time minting is no
longer needed. Collapsing is otherwise unchanged: same guard, same meet,
same recursion, so chains are still eliminated before the operand runs.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Drop the incremental map when a derived sampling target appears

Live typing adds sampling targets that no probe in the zipper accounts for --
`ids_with_unknown_types` -- and `IncrEval.reuse_check` cannot see them: its
per-node `probe_targets` cover placed probes only. So it reuses a slice that
was evaluated before one of those ids became a target, and the id comes back
with no samples: the live type is stale until some later edit forces the slice
to be re-evaluated.

EvalResult now tracks the derived targets (targets minus the placed probes)
alongside `cached_targets`. When they change while the elaboration does not --
toggling live typing being the clear case -- `prev_incr` is dropped so nothing
is reused. When the elaboration changed too, the normal incremental path
already re-evaluates what moved.

Known gap, as on oopsla2026 where this fix originated: a subtree whose
elab_syn_ty unknown-ness flips without its own elaboration changing could still
reuse stale samples. Believed hard to construct, since elaboration bakes type
changes into casts.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Compare the statics-refresh gate against placed probes, not all targets

`probes_differ` asked whether the zipper's probe ids equal `statics.targets`,
but `compute_targets` also derives targets from the program: probe_all's ids,
and live typing's unknown-typed ids. With live typing on, targets is therefore
strictly larger than the placed probes whenever any type has unknowns, the two
maps are never equal, and the gate reports a change on every frame -- so
`needs_refresh` is permanently true and every keystroke does a full
CachedStatics.init, bypassing the typing debounce.

The gate wants "did the probe set change since statics was built", so
CachedStatics now records the placed ids it was built from and the gate
compares against those. Equality still catches both additions and removals,
which a subset test against targets would not.

This is the local half of the Probes IV refresh gate: dev's version is correct
there because dev has no live typing, so targets and the placed probes coincide.

Prototype: keep the module-based HTML substrate as fast as the global one

Statics was ~3x and evaluation up to ~4x slower after the move to modules.
Four causes, each fixed at its source:

- Projecting Html.div substituted the 47-constructor sum for T. For a
  builtin module the member type keeps T as the path Html.T

  normalizing either.
- normalize_ctr_type kept only Var("HTML") compact; a builtin-module
  path is now compact too, so constructor annotations stay small.
- The evaluator substituted the module VALUE into every closure that
  named Html (80 copies in one program's output). A builtin module's
  member now elaborates directly to the constructor it denotes.

Ascriptions memoizes builtin path resolution. nutrient-rotation: analyze
2.8s (was 8.1s; baseline 2.3s), run 3.1s (was 11s; baseline 2.75s);
output size back to the baseline's.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Keep an unbound type variable's name through Typ.join

Restoring the alias meant not expanding through `Ctx.lookup_alias`, since its
stand-in hole for an unbound name would be read back as "the alias describes
the result" and resurrect the variable. Switching to `lookup_tvar` fixed that
but also dropped the name: `Unknown(Hole(Invalid("a")))` renders as `a`,
`Unknown(Internal)` renders as `?`, so join started losing information meet
keeps.

Expansion now yields the type to join against together with whether restoring
the name is meaningful. An unbound name joins against lookup_alias's hole, as
in meet, so the name survives; only a genuine Singleton is restorable.

An unbound type variable is not an error at this point -- statics reports those
separately as `TypFreeTypeVariable`, independent of this fallback -- so keeping
the name costs nothing and reads better than `?`.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Enable Typ.join's precision property, and fix what it found

The property -- join yields something at least as imprecise as both inputs --
was written but never registered, behind a TODO saying it did not hold for
forall and rec types. Enabling it turned up four distinct causes, only one of
which was about forall or rec.

A bug in the property itself: it normalized the two operands but not the join.
`normalize` resolves an unbound Var to a hole while join leaves it standing, so
any free type variable failed -- including join(T, T) against itself, e.g.
`(() -> x, () -> x)`. All three types are normalized now.

A real bug in join, which this fixes: `meet` deduplicates a product's repeated
labels before comparing, and join did not. A repeated label is ambiguous, so
dedup collapses it to one entry of unknown type; join compared the raw lists
and kept both, producing a shape meet would never return. Pinned as a unit
test rather than left to the generator.

Two shapes stay excluded, both because `is_more_precise` cannot judge them
rather than because join is wrong. It asks whether meet(a, b) gives back a,
and meet keeps the RIGHT operand's binder unconditionally, so
`meet(poly x -> t, poly ? -> t)` is never the left operand however precise it
is; Rec behaves likewise. Both live in meet, which this branch does not touch.

The property also surfaced a capture bug shared by meet and join: a variable
free in ty1 is swallowed when it happens to share a name with the other side's
binder, as in `(poly y -> x, poly x -> x)`. The adjacent note claims safety
because `subst` is capture-avoiding, but that covers renaming x1 to x2 inside
ty1, not the free variable the new binder captures. Left as a TODO on the meet
case; the property excludes it via the binder exclusion above.

Count drops from 100000 to 10000: the run cost 3s and the assumptions reject a
large fraction anyway, so the extra iterations bought little.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Preserve the alias in Typ.join, as Typ.meet already does

Both of meet's Var cases join against the alias's expansion and then check
whether the result came back as the expansion itself; if so they return the
original Var, so `meet(Pair, (Int, String))` is `Pair` rather than the
definition read out of the context. join expanded but never restored, so the
same call printed `(Int, String)`. Same concern as the `(_, Var(name))` case
in `Typ.diff`: don't hand back a node that came from the context when the
caller gave you an alias.

Expansion now goes through `Ctx.lookup_tvar` rather than `Ctx.lookup_alias`,
because the latter synthesizes an `Unknown` hole for an unbound name instead
of failing. join's `(Unknown(_), _)` arm returns that hole unchanged, so the
restore would have read it back as "the alias describes the result" and
resurrected the unbound variable -- `join(a, b)` for two unbound names would
have become `a`. Only a real Singleton is an expansion.

`init` accepted `Typ(_)`, but nothing downstream can serve it: `Info.typ`

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Don't collect ascription samples during pattern matching

`matches_inner` and `match_pattern` threaded the real targets into
`Ascriptions.transition_multiple`, which walks the writer and builds a sample
list, and then bound it to `_samples` and dropped it -- so the collection work
was wasted and a reader could not tell whether dropping it was deliberate.

Dropping is deliberate: the scrutinee reaches matching already final, so any
probe under its ascriptions has fired, at the call stack where evaluation
actually passed through it. Recording again here would double-count the same
values under whatever stack the match happens to run on. Passing
`Sample.no_targets` says that, and matches what Unboxing already does.

`match_pattern`'s `~targets` was only there to feed that call, so it goes.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Give the inferred dynamic type ids that name its own tokens

Statics builds the types it infers with `Typ.temp`, which stamps every node
with the `Id.invalid` sentinel. Rendered as-is the marks collapsed to that one
id, and `uniquify_repeated_tiles` minted fresh ids for every tile after the
first -- so all but one token was in no type and could not be marked. Worse,
whichever tile the renderer happened to emit first kept the sentinel, so on a
partially-known type the mark landed on a token statics had supplied:
`(fun x -> ^^statics((1, x)))(true)` coloured `Int` instead of `Bool`. It also
made `diff`'s wrapped_replaced test fire on any node sharing the sentinel with
a replaced one, marking the enclosing parens too. `Typ.replace_temp` already
existed for exactly this and had no callers.

The replacement goes where a type's ids become the ids of rendered tokens,
not where the type is inferred -- statics-built types reach this point from
more than one direction.

Also: `necessary_ids` had no `Sig` case, so an n-item signature's separators
were minted during rendering and could never be marked. It is `max(1, n)`,
the same as `Sum` -- rep_id for the braces plus one per `;`.

`Segment.tile_ids` is extracted next to `Segment.ids` rather than hand-rolled
a third time; it is the set of ids Code.re can actually class, since Grout and
Secondary carry none.

Tests go through `displayed_segment_and_marks` with `ProjectorInfo.utility` --
the composition the projector runs. A generator cannot find this: every
`QCheck_Util.arb_typ` node gets a distinct id, which is the one precondition
production violated.

- `(_, Var(name))` returned ids from the context's alias expansion, which are

- `(Parens(t1), Parens(t2))` dropped the dynamic parens' ids unconditionally,

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Mark the dynamic type by diffing the types the renderer renders

The type probe's Dynamic mode colours the parts of a type that came from
runtime. Parentheses were not coloured, so a wholly runtime-derived type
rendered half green: `let x : ? = (a=1) in ^^statics(x)` showed `(a=Int)`
with `a`, `=` and `Int` green and both parens in the static colour.

The marks are ids and Code.re colours a tile whose id is marked, so they
have to name the tiles the renderer emits. They could not name the parens,
because `typ_to_segment` does not render the type it is given: it desugars
Sig, then runs `parenthesize_typ`, which inserts parens as real Typ nodes
with fresh ids, and only then lays out tokens. Comparing the types as the
caller passed them cannot see nodes that do not exist yet.

So compare the normalized forms. `normalize_typ` is split out of
`typ_to_segment` and exposed, along with an entry point that renders an
already-normalized type -- normalization mints a fresh id per added Parens,
so it must run once and that one result must be both diffed and displayed.
The marking moves to DynamicTypInfer, taking both as injected functions
because ExpToSegment sits downstream of the projectors; ProjectorInfo
supplies them from one settings value so the two halves cannot disagree.

Typ.diff stripped parens before comparing, which is right for a semantic
comparison and wrong for naming rendered tokens. Parens now take the
verdict of the node they wrap: marked when that node is itself replaced,
left alone when it merely contains something that changed -- so
`(Int, ?)` vs `(Int, String)` still colours only `String`, while `?` vs
`(a=Int)` colours all of it.

PadIds is gone. Its id-count table moves into ExpToSegment beside the
`pad_ids` calls it mirrors, where it cannot drift, and two of its counts
were wrong: Sum padded one id too many, and MultiHole was treated as
needing one id when it needs one per gap.

`raise_if_padding` is gone too. It existed to catch that drift, but as a
field on the shared renderer settings threaded through nine modules, with
its only `true` in a test. The invariant it guarded -- a normalized type
carries every id its rendering consumes, so nothing is minted mid-render --
is now `ExpToSegment.typ_ids_sufficient` and a property over generated
types.

Test_PadIds becomes Test_DynamicTypMarks and tests the thing that matters
rather than that padding is idempotent: every mark appears in the render,
every colourable tile of a wholly runtime-derived type is marked, a type
runtime merely confirmed marks nothing, the padding invariant holds, and
unit pins for the id counts. The first two both failed before this change.

Verified in the browser: `(a=Int)` 5/5 tokens coloured and
`(a=(+ Zvb))` 8/8, against 3/5 and 4/8 before.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Split a tuple type's abbreviation budget across its components

Reported against a large list of labeled tuples: the type probe's widths
felt much coarser than the value probe's. They were.

`abbreviate_typ`'s Prod case mapped over its components with the shared
mutable budget -- a plain `List.map` with a `//TODO: abbreviate these like
tuples` on it -- so the first component took whatever it wanted and the
rest had nothing left and elided whole. Sweeping the budget over
`[(label=String, value=Float)]` shows it: every budget from 11 to 18
rendered `[(label=String, …)]`, one component in full detail beside one
that had vanished.

Components now share the budget evenly, which is what the exp walk already
does for a tuple via AbbrevBudget.split_evenly. The same sweep now
degrades both sides together -- `[(l…=…, v…=…)]`, `[(la…=…, v…=…)]`,
`[(lab…=…, va…=…)]` -- and yields 12 distinct widths where it used to
yield 8.

Explicit recursion rather than List.mapi: each child mutates the shared
budget, so evaluation order is load-bearing and List.map's is unspecified.

The test sweeps budgets 1-40 and pins both halves: at least 11 distinct

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Elide types to an ellipsis rather than to a type hole

Abbreviate shortened a type by replacing it with Unknown(Internal), which
prints as `?` -- a real type hole. So a type the abbreviator had cut looked
exactly like a hole the user still had to fill, and `(String, ?)` squeezed
down read as `(?, ?)`: the elided String and the genuine hole rendered the
same and there was no way to tell which was which.

Elision gets its own term, an unknown-with-invalid-hole carrying the
ellipsis, so the same type now reads `(…, ?)` -- shortened on the left,
still-to-fill on the right. This is the 23 elision sites inside
abbreviate_typ, so it applies wherever a type is cut: the type probe, and
types inside ascriptions in an abbreviated value.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Make the type probe resizable, sharing the drag with the value probe

Shift-drag across a type probe's cell now chooses how much of the type to
show, the way it already did for a probe's sample values.

The drag machinery moves to DragLength rather than being copied: the
pointer-capture dance, the guard for capture lost without a pointerup, the
cursor-to-column arithmetic, and the budget search. Only three things were
ever probe-specific in it, and none of them are the hard parts. Callers
keep their own pointerdown -- ProbeProj's carries pin, focus and
stop-propagation concerns unrelated to dragging -- and call begin_drag from
inside it. ProbeProj now delegates, so there is one implementation of the
capture guard instead of two.

`find_best_budget` needed no generalizing: it was already parameterized
over a measurement function, because the rendered width is not linear in
the budget -- Abbreviate is discrete -- so the budget that lands where the
cursor is has to be searched for rather than computed. The type probe
passes an abbreviate-and-measure over types (ProbeUtil.abbreviated_typ_seg_of,
the type analogue of the existing value one); the probe's block layout
passes width_is_budget, where the wrap width IS the budget.

No CSS. ProbeProj tags its cells with a width class from `length_cls`, but
the `--base` custom property those eight rules define is read by no
stylesheet and by no OCaml or JS -- so it sizes nothing, and the narrowing
is entirely the abbreviation rendering fewer characters. Left in place as a
pre-existing dead-CSS finding rather than removed here.

Verified in the browser: dragging `(String, ?)` inward gives `(String, ?)`
-> `(?, ?)` -> `?` across 12, 6 and 3 columns, and dragging back out
restores it.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Give the type projector a length, and Abbreviate a way to shrink a type

Groundwork for making the type probe resizable. No behaviour change yet:
nothing sets a length and nothing reads it.

`Abbreviate.abbreviate_typ` already existed as a 254-line recursion -- it
has to, since the exp and pat walks descend into ascriptions -- but had no
public `~available` entry point the way abbreviate_exp and abbreviate_pat
do. Adds one, mirroring theirs, plus the ellipsis term a type degenerates
to (an unknown-with-invalid-hole, which is what Typ.cls_of reads back as
Invalid).

TypeProj's model becomes {mode, length}. The length lives in the model
rather than in module-level state the way ProbeProj's sample lengths have
to: a sample is recreated every evaluation, a projector is not, so there is
no reason to reach for a global keyed by id.

`length` is a named variant, Auto | Fixed(int), not an option(int). The two
states are "as wide as the type needs" and "as wide as the user dragged
to", which option cannot say -- and it keeps Some/None out of the derived
reader, since those are shadowed in this scope (hence ProbeProj's
`Option.None`).

Reshaping a persisted model needs care: it is stored as a sexp and read
back at render time, where ProjectorBase.Cook calls deserialize_m with no
guard, so a raise takes the view down rather than resetting anything. The
reader is shadowed to be total, following CardProj and ProbeProj, and it
also reads the shape the model used to have -- a bare mode -- so an
existing projector keeps the mode the user toggled to instead of being
reset. Test_TypeProj pins all three: legacy models keep their mode, a
dragged length round-trips, and junk falls back rather than raising.

body:
Route the last web-side path handling through SlidePath

Two places in src/web still knew the separator or navigated a slide list
without it.

ScratchMode's top bar carried Previous/Next handlers that stepped by flat
`mod` over every slide, wrapping from the last back to the first with no
regard for folders. They have been unreachable since `~nav_buttons=false`
sits two lines above them, so this was pre-SlidePath logic kept alive by the
signal type. Scratch and Documentation are not getting arrows -- slides there
are reached through the breadcrumb dropdowns -- so the two branches now
return Effect.Ignore and say so.

TutorialText.title_of built a title by concatenating " / " itself. It now
composes the folders and leaf with SlidePath.mk, which drops the
`prefix == ""` special case, since mk with no folders is just the leaf. That
leaves no hardcoded separator anywhere in src/web outside two unrelated spots
(a separator glyph in ProbeSidebar, an "n / m" counter in ChatBottomBar).

title_of had no coverage -- it is the fallback for a lesson with no @title,
and all 28 set one -- so the change was to logic nothing exercised, and it is
not purely a refactor: for a path with a doubled separator the old code
produced "Basics /  / 01 - Holes". Empty segments are now filtered out rather
than becoming empty folders, and Test_TutorialText pins the derivation:
numbered lessons, the task/extra token, no leading number, one and two
subdirectories, and that doubled separator. Dropping the filter fails the
last case. Worth covering now, since filing a lesson in a subdirectory is how
it picks up a folder without an explicit title.

Also moves the folder-traversal properties out of Test_Tutorial, where they
were exercising SlidePath against production data rather than testing
anything about the lessons, into Test_SlidePath over its named fixtures. The
walk helper there is bounded by the size of the space: unbounded, a clamp
regression spun until the heap died instead of failing, which is a poor thing
to hand CI.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Give SlidePath an explicit API and address review

Adds SlidePath.rei. The type is abstract, so a path only exists by parsing a
name or building one from parts, both of which normalize -- which closes a
hole: Init.re was constructing `{folders: ["Derivations"], leaf: title}`
directly, so nothing stopped a segment holding a separator from producing a
path that would not render back to its own name. It now calls `mk`. Kept
internal: `separator`, `separator_char`, `same_folder` and `folder_indices`,
all pure implementation of the folder navigation. `depth` is deleted; it had
no caller but its own test.

Doc comments move to the .rei, each with a minimal example, and the nav
operations share one four-slide example space declared once in the header.
They describe what a path is rather than naming current call sites, and the
.re keeps only implementation notes so the contract is not written twice.

Other review fixes:

- `ListUtil.split_last` replaces the `List.rev`-and-match in `of_string`,
  which also removes its impossible empty-list branch.
- The separator is no longer written in two places: `separator` and
  `separator_char` sit together, one joined by `to_string` and one split on by
  `of_string`.
- No polymorphic equality: `List.equal(String.equal, ...)` in `same_folder`
  and in `breadcrumb`'s prefix comparison, `String.equal` in its dedup, and
  `equal` is derived rather than hand-written (`ppx_deriving.eq` added to the
  web library).
- `folder` returns `option(string)`, with None for a path that has no folder
  segment, rather than an empty-string sentinel.
- `step_in_folder`'s comment said "The index `by` steps from `current`", which
  parsed as nonsense; it now says what it does.

Tests: one suite per public function, and every navigation case names the
path it starts from ("Basics / Functions stays put") instead of a bare index,
with the example space's positions bound to names. Test_Tutorial gains an
id-uniqueness ratchet, which is what the README's claim that identity comes
from the id actually rests on -- the per-lesson store key is the id, so two
lessons sharing one would share saved work.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Mark read-only code in lesson prose as a display, not the editor

A locked cell in a lesson's prompt looked like the editor the student types
in, down to sharing its I-beam cursor. It now reads as a framed display.

The tint moves off `.code` and onto the cell. `.code` is only as wide as its
text, so it painted each line separately and ended ragged on the right with
the cell's surface showing through the gaps; on the cell it covers the result
row too. Its colour moves from --Y0 to --T1: --Y0 is the menu fill, and at
0.05 chroma it is twice the neutral ramp, which is what made it shout. --T1
puts these cells on the ramp that already exists -- page --SAND 99%, cell
--T1 97%, result strip --T3 91%.

The hairline is a box-shadow ring rather than a border. A border insets the
children while they keep the cell's own 6.4px radius, so their fill cuts
inside the curve and leaves a sliver at the bottom corners where the result
row rounds off; a ring draws outside the padding box, so the radius is shared
and the corners agree. No radius is set here at all -- `#main.Tutorial .cell`
already owns that value, and a class-only selector could not override it.

Locked cells get `cursor: default`. `#main .code-editor` gives the primary
editor an I-beam and was catching these too, so the cursor distinguished
nothing; the two locked panels were not even consistent with each other.
Text stays selectable so examples can be copied.

Inline code keeps --Y0 and is exempted from the cell rule: marking a token
inside a sentence is a different job from marking a read-only region, and the
two can diverge. The Task Reference panel is excluded as well --
`.task-reference-section` is already a card with this same fill and border,
and its body clips at exactly the cell's width, so a ring outside the cell
box survives only along the top edge.

body:
Replace Util.Either with result, and Core's Either where it is a partition

Our Either was `L | R` with show/sexp/yojson derivations that nothing
used -- no [@deriving] type in the tree embeds an Either.t. It also

'a it carried.

partition -- each element goes to the A-stream or the B-stream, neither
side an error -- so those take Core.Either's First/Second, and
src/util/Either.{re,rei} is deleted along with Util's re-export.

unrelated; it is untouched.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Use Core's list and option combinators where we hand-rolled them

Net -94 lines across 32 files. Follows the src/util idioms pass, now that
every library is opened over Core.

Deleted, having judged them not worth keeping:

  - ListUtil.rev_if -- a one-line combinator (b ? List.rev : Fn.id) with
    no Core equivalent, but `b ? List.rev(xs) : xs` at the call site reads
    better than a helper, and there were no call sites.
  - ListUtil.intersection_f -- the operation is reasonable but this
    implementation is O(n*m) over Poly.equal, which is a trap to leave
    lying around unused; the Core-idiomatic version would go through a
    Set. Both had tests and no production callers, so the tests went too
    (3323 -> 3320).

Kept but simplified, because Core has no equivalent for either:

  - StringUtil.trim_trailing_whitespace trims per *line*, which
    String.rstrip alone does not do. Its 22 lines of char-list reversal
    become String.rstrip(~drop=...) mapped over the split, 9 lines.
  - OptUtil.unzip distributes an option over a pair. Expressible as two
    Option.maps rather than a switch.

Replaced with Core combinators:

  - 42 List.length(x) == 0 / > 0 -> List.is_empty. Line-neutral but O(1)
    instead of O(n); several were on segment-scale lists.
  - 7 List.concat(List.map(...)) -> List.concat_map.
  - List.hd_exn(List.rev(x)) -> List.last_exn (2), List.map |> List.rev ->
    List.rev_map (1).
  - One switch in CardProj was a pure identity wrapper over its scrutinee
    and is gone entirely.
  - Three `| None => Some(z) | Some(z) => Some(z)` switches collapse to
    Some(... |> Option.value(~default=z)).
  - Three JSON field lookups in OpenRouter become Option.first_some.

On that last point: ocamlgrep finds 24 of those identity-Option-rewrap
switches, but only 7 are safe to convert. Option.first_some(a, b)
evaluates b eagerly, and most of the None branches here are recursive
calls (find_last_tile(rest), scan(tail)), monadic binds, or -- in
Measured.find_by_id -- a printf. Converting those would turn an
early-exit into unconditional work, so they stay as switches.

Migrate test/ to Jane Street Core

body:
Migrate src/language to Jane Street Core

Open Core over the language library, following src/util. Like util, the
library is the atomic unit: -open Core applies to the whole dune stanza,
so all 112 modules move together. 75 files touched, +2017/-1738.

Wiring matches util's -- flags on the library stanza so :standard keeps
inheriting dune-workspace's warning config, plus core in (libraries).

The bulk is mechanical: 538 labelled arguments (~f, ~init, ~compare), 102
typed equality witnesses, 31 List.is_empty / Option.is_some in place of
comparisons against [] and None, and 28 Stdlib.* prefixes.

The interesting part is the 67 conversions to _exn variants. Several
stdlib functions that raise have total counterparts in Core under the
same name, so the flip changes their return type rather than failing to
compile:

  - List.hd / tl / nth return options in Core. IdTagged.rep_id is
    List.hd(ids); under Core it silently became Id.t option and only
    broke at its use sites in MPat and Sig. Converted to hd_exn / tl_exn
    / nth_exn to keep the raising behaviour.
  - List.find likewise. Coverage.re had the raising stdlib find; it is
    find_exn now. The nine List.find_opt call sites are the ones that
    correctly become plain List.find.
  - List.map2 / for_all2 / fold_left2 / zip return Or_unequal_lengths
    rather than raising, so they became the _exn variants. Where the
    result was already being pattern-matched for length failure
    (combine_opt, map2_opt in util) the variant is better, but here the
    callers expect the exception.

Three shadowing traps, all silent under -open Core:

  - Local Map.Make / Set.Make now resolve to Core's comparator-based
    functors, whose interfaces differ. Ctx, Coverage, RuleVerify,
    LabeledTuple and BuiltinsTupleOperations get Stdlib. prefixes.
  - Float.modf returns a Parts record, not a tuple, and Core deprecates
    the top-level float primitives. BuiltinsBase backs Hazel's own float
    builtins, so those use Stdlib.ceil, Stdlib.sin, Stdlib.modf and so
    on -- exact behaviour rather than a plausible Core equivalent.
  - Int.max_int / min_int are max_value / min_value.

Equality is split deliberately. Where the type is concrete the witness is
named: String.equal, Id.equal, Bigint.equal, Option.equal, List.equal, or
the equal function [@deriving eq] already generates (equal_cls,
equal_op_bin, equal_projector_data, InvalidOperationError.equal,
DrvSort.equal). Int comparisons need nothing, since Core permits = on
int. That leaves whole-term and whole-record structural comparison, which
is what Poly is for: 26 explicit Poly.equal / phys_equal call sites, plus
open Poly in the four modules whose job is structural comparison --
Equality, MatchExp, DrvTermBase and Operators. Typ.re was kept under
Core's discipline and its six sites fixed individually, being the file
where an accidental equality would matter most.

The equality sites were found with ocamlgrep's typed patterns, which also
kept 33 hits out of the diff: [@deriving eq] synthesises equal functions
whose code is attributed back to the type declaration, so those matches
point at 'BadToken(string)' and 'time: float' rather than at any
comparison.

Public signatures are unchanged; haz3lcore, web and the CLI needed no
edits. make test-quick stays at 3323 tests and the release profile is
warning-free.

body:
CI: weekly Extended Tests, and test reports on the test job

Two changes to how CI reports and how far it searches.

Add .github/workflows/extended-tests.yml: weekly against dev, running the
whole suite through a new `make ci-extended` with qcheck-core's long mode on,
so every ~count is multiplied by QCHECK_LONG_FACTOR. The per-push suite runs
each property exactly once at its in-source count, which makes a property that
fails on one seed in a few hundred effectively invisible. The job fixes its
seed rather than letting qcheck self-init, and prints the whole QCHECK_*
command to its summary, so anything it finds reproduces verbatim. It gates
nothing.

Sizing the factor turned up that `Slow` is not a synonym for `QCheck`: most of
the suite's Slow-tagged tests are ordinary ones, so the factor scales a
minority of the run and the rest is a fixed floor. The default of 100 comes
from measuring that split rather than assuming it. The comments say so in
those terms and give the method for re-deriving it, because the measurements
themselves go stale -- as the `~32-min suite` and `~92%` notes removed here
had, badly enough to make factor 8 look like four hours when it was closer to
thirty minutes.

Separately, move the test reports off the Deploy job. checks.yml passed
`use-actions-summary: false` to dorny/test-reporter@v1, but that input does not
exist in v1 -- it was silently ignored and a check run was always created.
A check run belongs to a commit rather than to a workflow, and GitHub chooses
which of the commit's check suites it joins; it chose Deploy's, so test results
rendered under "Deploy branch preview" and a red suite made the deploy look
broken. On v3 the default writes the report to the job's own summary and
creates no check run, which is the only placement that is ours to pick.

Nothing is lost as a gate: `Fast checks` and `Full tests` already fail on a red
suite, and the report checks could never have been required anyway, since fork
pull requests skip them. With no check run to create, `checks: write` is no
longer needed, and the `publish-reports` input only gated Codecov -- renamed
to `upload-coverage`, and fork pull requests now get their reports too.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Standard library: group the builtins into modules, ship SHOW and ORD instances

Now that modules are real values the standard library can be one. `List`,
`String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Option` and `Pair` are module builtins, so the 65
list functions and the string family are reachable as `List.map` and
`String.length` instead of only as top-level `map` and `string_length`.

Every builtin keeps its flat name. `String.length` and `string_length` are
the same function, so no program, slide or exercise changes meaning; the
modules are the front door from here. Both halves of a module builtin are
derived from the same builtin records, the signature's member types and the
module's member values, so a member cannot drift from the function it names,
and a member is the implementation rather than a copy of it: it is the term
the flat name is bound to.

A module builtin is an ordinary constant whose type is a signature and whose
value is a module with already-evaluated items, because the environment
hands a program values: a module with pending items would arrive unevaluated
and its projections would not reduce. A member that holds a fixpoint still
has to unroll, so the projection now judges a definition the way a variable
lookup does, sharing one predicate. That is the only evaluator change, and
only a module out of the environment can hit it.

`SHOW` and `ORD` ship as signature types with an instance per base type
(`ShowInt`, `ShowFloat`, `ShowBool`, `ShowString`, `OrdInt`, `OrdFloat`,
`OrdString`), each with a manifest type member since resolution selects on
it. They are deliberately NOT ambient: a program marks what it wants, one
line per instance. Ambient instances are a language decision rather than a
library one and need a priority or coherence rule first, because with none a
program's own instance for a base type makes every call ambiguous against
the shipped one; twelve of the implicits tests change meaning if they are
ambient, which is the same warning from the other side.

No EQ: polymorphic `==` already compares two values of a type, so an
equality signature earns its keep only once a type can choose its own
equality, which wants the sharing constraint the docs already call for.

Tests: `Statics.BuiltinsModules` (11) on the signature side, member types,
a missing member, the signature aliases and instance resolution;
`Evaluator.BuiltinsModules` (10) on the value side, including that a member
equals its flat function and that a recursive member unrolls through a

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modular implicits (2/3): resolution at applications, marks, views

`implicit S : SIG` binders are implicit instances in their scope
(Ctx.ImplicitEntry, mark_implicit, implicit_instances). At an application
whose domain has implicit components (MatchedTyp.implicit_components), the
new Implicits.re decides how each is supplied: a literal tuple's items are
the components, and an implicit one takes the current item only when items
beyond the explicit ones remain and it is a module fitting the signature
(leftover items with a single explicit component make the whole tuple that
component's argument). It resolves the rest from the instances in scope, narrowed by the
explicit arguments' types and then the expected type, instantiates the
binders in the later components and the codomain (substitution by the
instance's path; avoidance when unresolved), analyzes the argument against
the instantiated explicit components and splices the instances into the
elaborated argument with ids derived from the application's, so the runtime
sees an ordinary application and incremental evaluation re-keys on it. A
tuple-typed argument that is not a literal is destructured around them.

Marks: ImplicitNotFound / ImplicitAmbiguous on the application (a hole is
passed so evaluation proceeds around the error), ImplicitBinderNotModule and
ImplicitBinderPosition on binders; Message.ImplicitResolved for the
inspector; CLI and inspector renderings. A failed resolution names the type
members the call requires of the instance, "no implicit instance of SHOW
with T = String": matching each component that mentions the binder against
the type supplied there, and the codomain against the expected type, reads
them off (Implicits.member_eqs). Both marks name the signature only when
there is one, so an unannotated binder no longer renders as a blank type.
`Fun` keeps its implicit binders nameable in the codomain and renames an
expected arrow's binders to the pattern's; the type checker scopes a
domain's binders over the later components and the codomain
(TypExpectation.ArrowDomainExpected).

Typ.ana_meet gains componentwise tuple subtyping (a module passed for an
implicit parameter arrives in a tuple) and treats an unknown arrow domain as
matching any domain.

Tests: Test_Statics_Implicits (39), Test_Evaluator_Implicits (15), an
elaboration pin of the spliced argument; has_mark_test and single_mark_test
move to the statics prelude. Three of those tests are one program written
twice: an implicit binder keeps the caller's type equation, while the same
parameter written plainly loses it to part 4's avoidance and checks the call
against nothing. The second is a pinned gap, documented as such here and in
docs/modules.md, not intended behavior.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Keep a printed `:` apart from a following operator

`Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` failed on `(()) @< ({ let _:+ Adid }) >`:
Menhir read the sig member as `_` ascribed to the sum `+ Adid`, MakeTerm read
it as a hole.

`:` is one of Token.ascii_operator_chars and Token.is_potential_operator
matches any run of them, so a `:` printed flush against a leading-plus sum
lexes as the single operator token `:+`, which is no form at all. Menhir has
its own lexer and splits them, hence the disagreement.

should_add_space already knew about this hazard -- it kept `:` apart from `$`
and `!` -- but as a list of two characters rather than the property they share.
It now asks Token.begins_with_potential_operator, which covers `!` along with
every other operator character. `$` stays listed: it is a name character, so
the predicate does not cover it.

An unparenthesized sum only reaches a `:` as a sig member's ascription, which
is why this appears from this part up and only on seeds that generate one.
The test prints once instead of round-tripping: Defensive parenthesization is
not idempotent on a Sig, so the text gains a paren layer every trip -- a
separate pre-existing bug, left alone here.

body:
Don't crash on a cyclic type alias

`type x = x.a in ?` aborted the whole analysis with
Failure("weak_head_normalize exceeded 1000 recursive calls").

TyAlias already guards self-reference by wrapping the definition in Rec, and
weak_head_normalize leaves a Rec alone. From this part up, though, `x.a` is a
module member projection, so normalizing it asks path_sig what `x` denotes, and
as_sig unrolls the Rec to look for a signature -- handing the projection
straight back to path_sig. Round and round until the fuel ran out, and running
out raised rather than degraded.

A cyclic alias has no weak head normal form, so out of fuel the type now comes
back unreduced: stuck, which is what this function already returns for anything
else it cannot reduce. Callers that need a real head then report a type error
the ordinary way -- the program now says "Expected a module or tuple type, found
type rec x -> x.a", matching what dev says for the tuple-projection reading of
the same syntax.

Only the previously-crashing path changes: any type that reduced within the fuel
budget reduces identically.

CI found this through the Slow `Elaboration does not crash` property, so it hit
only on runs whose seed generated such an alias -- red on parts 5-8, green on 4
and 9, all on this one bug. Test_Typ pins it deterministically instead.

body:
Incremental eval: a binding's ascription is part of its provenance

Editing `module M : S = ...`'s signature left dependents of M reusing
values computed under the old signature: the reuse provenance recorded
only that the binding went through an ascription, not which type. Since
an ascription changes the bound value (sealing a module, casting), the
type now travels in the provenance (`Ascribed(Typ.t)`) and is compared
with `Typ.fast_equal`.

Regression test: dropping a member from a module's signature invalidates
the cached use of that member.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Coverage: a stuck path type is opaque, not non-normalized

Since abstract type members, a path `m.T` survives normalization. The
coverage checker's column functions (prepend_ctr, cons_from_type,
prepend_from_type) still treated ProdProjection as a non-normalized type
and failed on `case m.x | ...` with `m.x : m.T`. A stuck path is now opaque
like a type variable: only a wildcard or variable pattern exhausts it
(all_ctrs_of_type already said so). Two regression tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: an escaped abstract type instead of a silent unknown

Avoidance minted `?` where a path outlived its root, and `?` is consistent
with everything, so the loss was silent: nothing told the author, and every
later use type-checked against nothing. It now mints the escaped abstract
type from the previous commit, and the three shapes that lost their types
report where they are used:

  let get = fun (m : BOX) -> m.x in get(B) + 1
  -- This has the abstract type m.T, which escaped the scope of its module,
     so it cannot be used where a concrete type is required

  let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in dup(ShowInt, "s")
  -- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that
     type; mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest
     signature, to keep the caller's type

Binding one, passing it to an unannotated function and giving it to a hole
all still work, which is the gradual half of the bargain: the type is
consistent with `?`, so the error appears where the author wrote something
concrete.

The `Fun` arm now closes the parameter as well as the body. A component
annotated `x : m.T` says nothing to a caller, who cannot name `m`, and
leaving it open meant the type mentioned a binder out of scope and every
argument passed, since normalization maps a path with an unbound root to
unknown. Only the copy that becomes the function's type is closed; the
pattern's own type and the elaborated ascription keep the precise path, so
runtime casts and incremental-evaluation keys do not move.

Where an escaping path becomes an escaped type rather than plain unknown is
a parameter of avoidance (`Typ.escape_to`), because one caller wants the old
behavior: an implicit binder that resolution could not supply is already
marked, so opacity there would only cascade.

Escaping is generative per application (`Typ.freshen_escaped` at `Ap`): two
calls of one function escape different types, so joining them is an error
naming both, while a value bound once and used twice is not. Identities are
derived from the application's id rather than generated, so re-checking an
elaboration still yields an equal type; `Statics.Properties` covers that and
the closedness property.

`Mark.EscapedType` says which side escaped, so the advice fits the case:
a required type suggests the implicit binder or a manifest signature, a
supplied one says the value cannot be used concretely, and two different
escapes of one path say so rather than printing the same name twice. An
escaped type displays as its path plus a short tag of its identity for the
same reason. A tuple argument still reports the component and the tuple:
that is the pre-existing cascade (`f(true, 1)` on plain Ints does it too),
fixed off-stack in #2502.

Tests: five cases in Statics.Modules (concrete use, unannotated use, the
generative join, the join with itself, the dependent parameter), the equal
mark arm, and the escape tests now assert the escaped type where they
asserted unknown. Slide item 42 keeps its abstract type and 43 shows the
error; docs/modules.md documents the type, generativity and the dependent
parameter.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules II (2/4): width subtyping at analysis positions

- `Typ.ana_meet`/`Typ.sig_sub`: where an expression is analyzed against a
  type, a signature fits a signature declaring a subset of its members
  (the wider one's type members are opened under fresh names), value
  members may themselves be wider, and functions are contravariant in
  their domain. Exact `meet` is tried first and stays the consistency
  relation for joins, equality and `is_consistent`.
- `StaticsBase.fixed_typ`/`expectation_mismatch_mark`/`syn_ana_ok_common`
  route through `ana_meet`, with `_pat` variants swapping the required and
  provided roles for pattern checks. Returning the expected type is what
  seals a binder.
- `ModuleExtraMembers` retired: extra members are sealed away. Hole-named
  signature members no longer cause an error.
- Dynamics: the last binding step (or a discard that leaves nothing
  pending) yields the module value marked final, so evaluated bindings are
  never re-traversed; re-traversal double-sampled probed literals.
- Tests for width in let/asc/module/function-argument/bound-variable/nested
  positions, contravariance, the exact-join boundary, `Typ.AnaMeet`,
  runtime sealing and probes. Slide section E showcases width subtyping
  (structural interfaces, hiding helpers, depth, contravariance, joins).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: an abstract member cannot be named through a signature alias

`type S = { type T; … } in let y : S.T = …` used to type `S.T` as `?`: the
alias names no module, so there is no particular T to name, and the
gradual escape let any value pass while the inspector called `?` an
abstract type. It is now an error on the label (`TypAbstractMemberOfSignature`),
with the dot explaining that a module M of the signature names it as
`M.T`; TyDi no longer suggests such members. Manifest members through an
alias, and abstract members through a module path, are unchanged.

Also: a type path rooted at a base type (`Nat.T`, where a module happens
to share the type's name) now says that the name is a base type, not a
module, instead of a generic tuple-type message.

Slide item 36a; tests for the alias error, the module route, manifest
members, and a missing member through an alias.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: an escaped abstract type, inert

`Typ.Escaped({id, label})` is an abstract type whose path lost the binder it
was rooted at. Its identity is the id: two escaped types are the same type
only when their ids agree, so it is consistent with itself and, through the
existing Unknown cases of `meet`, with `?`, and with nothing else. That is
the relation an in-scope abstract member already has, so no rule is invented
here; what is new is a representation that survives the loss of its root.

It is closed. `path_roots` and `free_vars` return nothing for it, which is
why the alternative of leaving the open path in place is not viable: part 4's
own property that a root type mentions no internal binder has to keep
holding. The label is provenance for display only, never traversed as a
type.

`Typ.freshen_escaped(~site, ty)` derives a new identity for each distinct
escaped type from the site and the old id. It is what gives each application
site its own abstract types in the next commit, and deriving rather than
generating keeps a type stable across statics passes, which re-checking an
elaboration depends on.

Nothing mints one yet, so no program changes meaning. The rest is arms:
`meet` (the only semantic ones), traversals in Typ, `Equality`, `Abbreviate`,
`Substitution`, the four opaque groups of `Coverage` next to a stuck path,
the printer and its precedence, and the unreachable arms that keep exhaustive
matches total in `Statics.utyp_to_info_map`, `Conversion` and `ExplainThis`.
The form is internal, so there is no lexer, tile, parser or round-trip work.

Tests: a `Typ.Escaped` group covering the meet rules, symmetry, idempotence,
`?`-consistency, distinctness, closedness, identity under normalization and
avoidance, printing, and freshening.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Editor: downgrade a signature type item when its = is deleted

Deleting the `=` of a signature `type T = Int` left an incomplete `type`
tile waiting for `=`, so the item read as a hole rather than an abstract
member. `Destruct` now runs `Insert.downgrade_bare_sig_type`, the inverse
of the `=` upgrade: an incomplete signature `type _ = _` tile with only its
`type` shard becomes the bare form again. The old definition is left
dangling as a stray type, to be removed or reattached by retyping `=`. A
module-body `type T = _` has no bare form and is unchanged.

Editing.SigAbstract grows to 34 cases covering typing the bare form,
adding `=` in every position, removing it (backward, forward, by
selection, with a following item, hole or compound definition, inside a
module annotation), round trips, and a MakeTerm-level check of the
resulting item kinds, since the printer shows a bare tile and an
incomplete `type T =` tile alike.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: report a missing member once, and let signatures name sibling members

The synthetic `x : T` expectation checked inside a module body reused the
signature's own type nodes, so a module missing `type T` reported "T is
not bound" on the signature as well as the missing member on the module.
A member whose declared type mentions a signature name the module does not
define now gets no expectation (the missing member is reported on the
module), and expectations carry fresh ids, so checking them never records
info under the signature's nodes.

Signature items also could not see earlier value or module members, so
`{ module Inner : { type T }; let y : Inner.T }` was rejected on its own.
`Ctx.extend_sig_item` binds those members as variables, threaded through
normalize, meet, equal_up_to_aliases and sig_sub; in sig_sub a sibling is
bound to the type the module provides, the way an abstract T is realized
by the module, so `y : Int` satisfies `y : Inner.T` when `Inner.T = Int`.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules II (4/4): module-typed functions and generative escape

- `Typ.avoid(ctx, ~escaping, ty)` at function bodies, let bodies (hence
  `module ... in`) and case arms: a module path rooted at a binder going
  out of scope is reduced in the body's context (manifest members simply
  expand); one still abstract becomes `?`, except that a signature member
  defined as that path becomes abstract and later members refer to it by
  name. `fun (m : S) -> m : S -> S`, `fun (m : S) -> m.x : S -> ?`, and
  each call of a function returning a module with abstract members yields
  a fresh type. Inside the scope `m.x : m.T` is unchanged; the C3 tests
  that pinned root types now read the in-scope type from the info map.
- Signature walk binds value member names too, so a member typed by a
  sibling module's abstract type projects as `M.Inner.T` rather than `?`;
  `path_sig` falls back to a written-out signature, so `{ type T = Int }.T`
  (left behind by type alias substitution) projects.
- Dynamics: a cast to an abstract path type is a no-op (manifest paths are
  normalized away before runtime); `let z : m.U = m.y` no longer leaves a
  stuck `1:m.U`.
- QCheck: the AST generator emits signature types (with a shrinker); new
  property "Root type mentions no internal binder".
- The Modules doc slide is split: `modules.hz` (construction, qualified
  types, signatures, errors) and `module-signatures.hz` (width subtyping,
  abstract types, module-typed functions, new section G). One slide of
  both was at the JavaScript stack limit: jsoo statics overflows node's
  default stack at roughly 100 nested lets, and the combined slide needed
  984-1000KB.
- Tests: Statics.Modules (17 cases), Typ.Avoid, Evaluator.Modules,
  Elaboration, MakeTerm, Menhir, round-trip; docs/modules.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules II (3/4): abstract type members, sealing, path types

- `type T` with no definition is a signature item (`SigTypeAbstract`):
  grammar, Sig member view (`TypeAbstract`), tile form (listed before the
  manifest form so `type` expands to it in a signature), MakeTerm, Menhir
  `sigItem`, printers, equality, abbreviation, ExplainThis.
- Sealing: a module analyzed against `{ type T; let x : T }` must define
  T (a missing definition is a missing member; a value named T does not
  count) and its members are checked against its own definition.
  `Typ.sig_sub` realizes an abstract member of the required signature by
  whatever the module provides; a manifest member is not satisfied by an
  abstract one. `meet` matches abstract with abstract only.
- Path types: an abstract member projected from a module path is the stuck
  normal form `M.T`, consistent with itself and `?` only. `Typ.path_sig`
  returns the path; `weak_head_normalize`, `normalize` and `meet` stop at a
  stuck path. A module variable's type is strengthened (`Typ.strengthen`)
  so `M.x : M.T` and `module N = M` shares `M.T`, while separately sealed
  modules have distinct types. Non-path projections and signature aliases
  give `?`. `Message.PathAbstract` reports `M.T` in the cursor inspector.
- Editor: typing `=` after a bare `type T` upgrades the tile to the
  manifest form (`Insert.upgrade_bare_sig_type`); no downgrade.
- Dynamics: runtime sealing ascribes members to their closed types, so an
  abstract member casts to `?` instead of leaving a stuck `v:T`.
- Tests: Statics.Modules, Typ.SigPaths, Evaluator.Modules,
  Editing.SigAbstract, MakeTerm, Menhir, round-trip, TyDi, Equality.
  Slide section F (Counter) and docs/modules.md describe the design.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: a module wins over a constructor of the same name in dot position

A capitalized module name parses as a constructor, and a known constructor
took precedence, so a module whose name matched one could not be projected
at all. The JSON type contributes `List`, `Int`, `String`, `Float` and
`Bool` to every program's constructor namespace, which made those five
names unusable as modules:

  module List = { let f = 1 } in List.f    -- Expected a module or tuple

The `Dot` arm now reads a bare constructor as a variable when a module of
that name is in scope, the same rewrite the `Constructor` arm already does
for a name that is not a constructor at all. Projecting a constructor means
nothing, so nothing is lost, and a constructor of the same name still
applies: `List([Int(2)])` is still JSON.

Two tests: the module is projected, and the constructor still builds a JSON
value in the same program.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: a member name is a label, so substitution shadows it

The `Module` case of `Substitution.in_exp` already refused to rename the
names bound by evaluated bindings and by module declarations, for the reason
its comment gives: they are member names. A pending `ModLet` went through
`in_pat` anyway, which renames a binder away from capture, so the member
label changed and `M.x` stopped finding it.

It shadows now, like the other two. The stepper substitutes the whole
builtin environment (`StepperView`), so before this any module with a member
named after a builtin lost that member: `{ let map = … }` became
`{ let map' = … }` and the projection was stuck.

Two tests: a member keeps its name where an ordinary binder would be
renamed, and a later item sees the member rather than the substitution.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Tests: pin the `:+` printer divergence between menhir and MakeTerm

An ascription immediately followed by a sum prints as `:+` with no space,
and the editor lexes that as one operator token, so MakeTerm yields a
MultiHole where menhir reads `Asc(_, Sum)`. Spacing it as `: +` parses the
same both ways, and reprinting the spaced form is not stable either, so the
printer is the trigger.

Four cases: the two diverging programs, skipped with the reason, and their
spaced forms, which must keep passing and are what the printer should have
produced. Nothing here is about signatures; a signature member is only how
the QCheck generator reaches the shape, which is why `Menhir and maketerm
are equivalent` fails per-seed from part 4 up (reproduce with
QCHECK_SEED=803422318).

Modules: the function shorthand binds a member

`let f(x) = ...` in a module body exported `x` rather than `f`: the body's
binders were read with Pat.bound_vars, which treats an applied pattern as a
constructor application. The lowering now reads a let item's binder through
FunctionSugar.binder, and annotates a shorthand at its name with the type
its signature expects; the Let case of statics then desugars it exactly as
it does a top-level shorthand. FunctionSugar accepts the ascribed name as
the head of the sugar for that purpose.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules: module-aware projection errors, one error per differing type member

Projection errors on modules now follow the design the type-level `M.Fake`
already had: the label carries the error and the dot only a message.

- `m.y` with no member y marks the label with `ModuleMemberNotFound` (which
  also says when y is a type member being used as a value) and gives the
  dot the message `Message.ModuleMemberNotFound`; the dot is no longer red.
- `M.T` in a type with no type member T marks the label with
  `ModuleTypeMemberNotFound`, naming the module's type members (or that it
  has none); the same for a missing sub-module in `M.P.T`. The type-level
  traversal passes `ModuleMemberExpected` for module paths, so TyDi still
  completes members. `m.T` where m is a value that is not a module gets
  `TypWantModule`, which names m's type.
- The dot marks that said "tuple" now say "module or tuple", in the CLI
  and the cursor inspector.
- A manifest type member that differs from the signature is reported once,
  on its `type` item. Member expectations keep a type member the module
  defines as its own definition (`Typ.sig_project_value ~keep_local`),
  so `let x = true` is fine when the module says `type T = Bool`, and the
  module is not reported a second time as a whole (it takes the declared
  type, as its binder does). Expectations also carry fresh ids so they
  never record info under the signature's own type nodes.

Tests for each attribution; slide items 11a-11d show the new messages.

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Modules II (1/4): first-class signature types and module values

Replace the labeled-tuple gloss with real module statics and dynamics.

Statics:
- `Sig` is a distinct first-class type; `Typ.desugar_sig` is gone and
  `Sig`/`Prod` are inconsistent both ways. Signatures are dependent
  records: `free_vars`, `subst`, `normalize` and `meet` treat type members
  as sequential binders; `meet` requires the same member names (exact,
  no width yet). `Sig.re` exposes the member view.
- A module synthesizes its signature in source order (`ModuleHelpers.
  module_sig_type`); manifest type members in an analyzed signature are
  checked (`ModuleTypeMemberMismatch`) and substituted into member
  expectations; missing members mark the module (`ModuleMissingMembers`).
- `M.T` resolves through the module variable's signature (`Typ.path_sig`,
  incl. `M.P.T`, aliasing and signature aliases); the `Let`-case
  `TVarEntry` injection is removed. `Dot` projects signature members.

Dynamics:
- Modules evaluate as modules: `Transition.re` steps `Module(items)` item
  by item with sequential scoping; evaluated bindings become the
  dynamics-only item `ModVal(x, v)`, and a module of `ModVal`s is a value.
  `Dot` reads bindings by name; ascribing a module value to a signature
  seals it. New `EvalCtx.ModuleItem`/`ModuleVal` contexts.
- Elaboration refolds the checked Let/TyAlias chain back into a `Module`.

Also: TyDi qualified completions read signature members, cursor inspector
and ErrorPrint render the new marks, docs and the Modules slide updated,
tests migrated (module types are signatures, module values are modules).

body:
Remove dead CSS rules and unreferenced assets

22 rule blocks (135 lines) across 9 stylesheets, 12 unreferenced icons, and
style/palette.html -- a design swatch page nothing links to and no dune rule
copies into the build.

This is the one change in the cleanup that no compiler can check, so the
liveness test is deliberately over-cautious. A selector counts as LIVE if any
of the following holds:

  - its name appears as a string literal anywhere in src/ or test/
  - some literal is a prefix of it, since classes get concatenated:
    "depth-" ++ string_of_int n, "agent-md-h" ++ string_of_int level,
    "highlight-code-" ++ c, "slash-card-" ++ kind

    the DOM through show/to_string and never appear as a literal at all, which
    is what .Mod, .Sig, .MPat, .Rul, .EmptyHole and .Single are. A naive
    literals-only scan called all of those dead.

re-checked by hand with a direct grep for both the hyphenated and underscored
spelling. .call-cursor was dropped from the list on that check -- there is a
call_cursor in source.

the key (rightmost) compound: `.projector.probe .window-toggle` can only match

author: Alexander Bandukwala
body:
Add .rei interfaces for 12 src/util modules

This is the ratchet half of the cleanup. The index-based detector finds dead
code once; a .rei keeps it from coming back, because warning 32 is a hard
error in the release profile that deploy_branches.yml gates on. No build
configuration change is needed -- the module just has to have an interface.

Chosen on how many lines of type declaration each one makes you maintain in
two places, not on file size:

  ListUtil 64, JsUtil 60, StringUtil 27, Unicode 25, Tree 23, OptUtil 19,
  Aba 18, VarMap 9, StructureShareSexp 8, Direction 5, Either 4,
  FloatingElement 2

264 lines of interface, of which 23 are restated types. Deliberately excluded:
Menu (70 lines of type restatement) and OpenRouter (101) -- for those, inline
`module M: { ... } = { ... }` sealing gets the same warning-32 coverage with
the signature written once, and Id.re:142 already does it. Also every
`include <third-party>` module (BigInt, Sets, Maps, MapUtil, IntMap, Result),
where the interface is 4-10x the source and re-breaks on the dependency's next
release, and Util.re itself, which dune treats as the library interface module.

Immediate payoff beyond prevention: Tree.equal_struct and, once it went,
Tree.equal were both dead. Neither was reachable by the index tool -- both
match its ppx-name suppression (^equal), which exists because ppx-generated
call sites are absent from the index entirely. The two mechanisms have
complementary blind spots, which is the argument for running both.

Interfaces are narrowed to each module's actual external surface, so a value
used only inside its own module is now private and warning 32 watches it from
here on. E.g. JsUtil hides 12 helpers (date_now, find_scroll_container,
QueryParams.get_arguments, ...) that no other module calls.

Tooling: scripts/gen_rei.sh + `make rei FILE=...` generate a starter interface
by running `ocamlc -i` over the ppx-expanded source dune has already built,
then refmt. Output is refmt-clean, so @src/fmt accepts it. It strips the
library's own alias prefix, which -short-paths would otherwise render as
`Util.Either.t` inside src/util -- a dependency cycle when compiled as a .rei.

dropdown of anyone who had been there before -- which looks exactly like
a broken build and is not one. A fresh profile against the same URL
listed it, which is what separated the two.

The naive fix, unioning the saved list with the defaults, trades this bug
for a worse one. Users really can delete slides: DeleteSlide, with a
confirm dialog warning the code is gone for good. A union resurrects
every deleted slide on the next load, permanently, which makes deletion
impossible rather than merely awkward. So slide_meta gains
known_defaults, the shipped names this browser has already been offered.
Absent from names but present there means deleted on purpose; absent from
both means never seen. Only the second kind splices in.

Each new slide is anchored to the nearest default ahead of it that this
browser actually has, and emitted just after. That puts slide 0 before
1. Values rather than at the end past Derivations, and it keeps the
choice sensible when the saved list has been reordered, where "default
order" is otherwise ambiguous. Saved order, renames and user-added slides
stay put; current follows its slide by name rather than by index.

Scratch does not reconcile. Its default is a seed, Scratchpad 1, not
shipped content, so splicing it back would hand a fresh empty pad to
everyone who had renamed or deleted theirs. Only doc passes
~reconcile=true.

One cost, once: a meta written before this existed has no
known_defaults, so it is seeded from the defaults still present, and a
documentation slide deleted before the upgrade comes back a single time.
A pre-upgrade meta cannot distinguish deleted from never-offered, and
getting new slides to appear at all seemed worth it. load_all now also
records the shipped list on a first visit, so deletions made after this
are exact.

pre-upgrade meta of 86 names, no slide 0, no known_defaults, sitting on
2. Symbols, reloaded to 0-8 with the selection still on Symbols; then
slide 7 removed from names with known_defaults left intact stayed gone
across a reload. Test_SlideReconcile covers ordering, deletion,
reordering, current tracking, the pre-upgrade seed, idempotence, and the

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Record what the export-diff check missed, and the edge-cache hazard

Two things learned since this document landed, both from the session working
on Fumola's web-play page.

fumola#74 did break something. Not in Hazel -- the "blast radius: none" line
holds -- but in pages/web-play/index.html, and the check that produced that
line could not have found it. `importsOf` decided a path was absolute by
testing for a `/`, correct while a bare name meant a symlinked neighbour and
wrong the moment deleting the symlinks gave every relative path a slash.
Opening an example body failed with ModuleFileNotFound("../system/adapton").

Nothing about the API changed. The export list was identical, all six of
Hazel's calls resolved, every check passed, and the feature was broken. What
changed was the shape of data flowing through an unchanged interface. So the
export diff catches a changed signature and is blind to a changed convention,
which is the class a generated fixture would catch and a hand-transcribed one
never will. Recorded as an addendum where a reader meets the original claim,
rather than quietly softening it.

And a hazard for anyone verifying a deploy: the edge served a pre-deploy
object inside its own max-age=600 window. A fetch just after a successful
deploy returned bytes byte-identical to the pre-deploy copy; a minute later
the same URL returned the new object with X-Cache: MISS. A deploy was nearly
reported as half-broken on the strength of the first read. Check X-Cache and
content, not the status code, and re-fetch before concluding.

That is the same failure content-addressed URLs remove for page loads, but the
unversioned URLs stay published for older clients, so verifying through them
keeps the hazard.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Merge #2509: load the Fumola runtime by content hash

The published runtime is served from stable URLs, so a browser that has the
5.6 MB binary keeps it. After a Fumola deploy a livelit can run against a
runtime a version behind, which looks like a bug rather than a cache.
Adapton/fumola#69 fixes that at the source by publishing each build to a
content-addressed directory named by a manifest; this is the consumer side.

WHAT CHANGED

`prebundle.js` reads `<origin>/runtime.json` before importing, and takes the
glue and the binary from the directory it names. Both or neither: wasm-bindgen
emits them as a matched set and they do not load if their versions disagree,
so a half-applied manifest would be worse than ignoring one.

A published origin stays ONE source with one timeout budget rather than
becoming two entries. Doubling the source count would double the worst case a
page waits before reporting the runtime unavailable -- currently 90s across
three sources.

No manifest, or one that does not parse, falls through to the unversioned pair
at the origin root, which is that origin's current build at publish time. That
is also the path for an origin published before manifests existed -- which is
every origin today, so this can land before Fumola deploys. Verified against
the live fumola.org, which has no runtime.json: the loader falls back, reports
`fumola.org @ stable`, and evaluates correctly.

WHICH FUMOLA IS THIS PAGE HOLDING?

`window.fumola.source()` now answers with the version as well as the origin:

    "fumola.org @ 290846d3aad19d38"   the current build, by content hash
    "fumola.org @ stable"             manifest unreachable; the root pair
    "local @ stable"                  your own build-fumola-wasm.sh

That question was previously unanswerable from a browser, and it is the first
one worth asking when a livelit misbehaves for someone and not for you. It
also removes the need for a `fumola_version()` export compiled into the wasm:
the manifest is the version stamp.

Verified with the real bundle (esbuild over prebundle.js) in a browser,
against a locally published site: the loader requests runtime.json, then the
hashed glue and hashed binary, and `` `x := 41; get(`x) + 1 `` returns 42.

THE DOC

docs/fumola-runtime-changes.md is new, and is the reason this was looked at.
Hazel pins no version of Fumola -- no submodule, no revision, no lockfile
entry -- so a change merged there reaches every Hazel user without any commit
here, and nothing in Hazel's CI notices. The doc records the dependency
precisely, an event log starting with fumola#74, and a four-tier testing
methodology.

Its least comfortable finding: nothing in either repository tests a Fumola
livelit against a live runtime. `Evaluator.Livelit` skips all four outright,
`FumolaValue` and `FumolaSource` feed hand-written JSON fixtures and would
pass with the wasm deleted, and `prebundle.js` has no test at all. Those
fixtures are the only written record of the two repos' agreement and they are
transcribed by hand, so a reply-shape change in Fumola leaves them passing
while asserting the old shape. Generating them from the runtime is the first
item that would close it, and needs no browser.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Do not let one stalled source hold up the runtime

A source that fails is fine: the loop moves on. A source that hangs is not.
Nothing in fetch or import times out on its own, so a source that stalls at
the TCP or TLS level -- rather than refusing -- parks the loop forever. No
later source is tried and no event is dispatched, which is the same stuck
"still loading" the event was added to end, reached by a different road.
That was a narrow risk with one published source; with three, and the first
of them mid-DNS-propagation, it is worth closing.

The budget is generous, because a slow connection is not a broken one and
the wasm is several megabytes. An overrunning source is set aside rather
than cancelled: if it lands later and nothing else has won by then, it is
still the runtime we wanted, so it is taken and announced.

The `abandoned` flag is load-bearing, and testing found out why. The late
claim is attached before the one inside withTimeout, so it runs first, while
wasm is still null -- without the flag it also fires on the ordinary path,
claiming a perfectly timely load as a late one and dispatching a second
event for it. Conditioning it on the search having actually moved on is what
keeps the late path to the case it is for.

Verified against a server that accepts connections and never answers: with
it first in the list, the loader waits out its budget, falls through to the
next source, and the card resolves -- one claim logged, none of them late.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Recover when the Fumola runtime finishes loading

The runtime is several megabytes of wasm, usually fetched cross-origin, so a
program is routinely elaborated before it exists. Such a program is not
wrong -- its Fumola livelits expand to "the runtime is still loading", which
was true when it was said -- but nothing ever revisited it. The card stayed
that way for the life of the page, and since card 0 is the one a cold
visitor lands on, that is the state they saw.

Three things were in the way, and each had to be moved:

  The shim never said anything. It now dispatches an event once the outcome
  is settled -- on failure too, so the message can settle from "still
  loading" to "unavailable" rather than waiting on a load that is not
  coming.

  Statics are rebuilt only for an edit. There was no edit, so the listener
  sets the same force_on_next flag the modes set for RefreshStatics, and
  sends Refresh to make a calculate pass happen at all.

  Elaboration is memoized on the term, and the term did not change. This is
  why forcing statics was not enough, and why editing the card did not help
  either: an unedited zipper yields an equal term and hits the cache. So the
  memo key now carries a generation, and the listener bumps it. Core.Memo
  has no way to clear an entry, which is why the key carries this instead.

Verified by making the race deterministic -- an artificial delay before the
runtime is published to the page -- and watching a card go from "the Fumola
runtime is still loading" to (6, 42, "adapton(settings)") on its own, with
no reload and no edit. Instrumented once to confirm all three fire in order:
the callback, then StaticsForce, then a recompute at the new generation.

this file hard-coded works before the switch and not after, and the new
one works after and not before.

build stays first, so working on Fumola and Hazel together is unchanged.

author: disconcision
body:
agent: one statics pass per tool call; member chunks fast-parse; phase timers

Measured on the dungeon run-2 replay (170 lines, 100 nodes), per tool call:

- Statics ran four times per tool (composition initial + new, editor
  re-init, canvas snapshot) and twice more in the Update diff. Now one:
  CachedStatics keeps a small ring keyed by a fingerprint of the program's
  piece ids (secondaries left out — whitespace passes keep it; object
  identity and MakeTerm term-equality both failed to survive the trip).
  The tool path computes the new program's statics the editor's way and
  offers them; CodeWithStatics, the canvas snapshot and mk_diff take the
  offer. AgentPulse moves to util so core can read the burst mask.
- Module-member chunks (`;`-prefixed) fell to the quadratic typing parser
  on every insert; the separator is split off, the member fast-parsed,
  the `;` spliced back as a tile. 27 fallbacks → 0 on the replay.
- Materialize.all only when the chunk mentions a `^^` trigger.
- The Update diff selected each side against the old syntax table and
  Move.jump_to_side_of_id token-walked to the buffer extreme and back
  (~0.7 s per selection); each side now uses its own CachedSyntax and the
  jump has a structural fast path (Zipper.unzip_to_id), walk as fallback.
- Util.PerfTimer: phase timers (statics, editor-statics/<trigger>,
  tool/handler|diff|snapshots, parse/splice/reformat, edit-action
  attribution); the journal's perf-tool: line carries the summary.

Numbers and rounds: plans/agent-perf.md "Results, round by round".

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Split the Fumola card into a textbook, one chapter at a time

One card had grown to cover everything from integers to the adapton event
log. It is now eight, in successive complexity: values, then how they are
named, then the state that makes editing incremental, then thunks, then the
way in, then the runtime itself -- and then the examples from the Fumola repo
that have something to run.

Chapters 1 to 6 are the old card's sections moved verbatim rather than
retyped, so nothing was lost in transcription. Each stands alone, which is
the point of a chapter, so each opens with the same short reminder of the
four livelits.

Chapter 4 is written fresh: the forcing section used to force thunks the
values section had made, which does not survive being separated. It makes
its own four thunks and forces them from a separate livelit, so the pairs
line up in the result.

Chapter 8 covers time, and makes the two claims the Extended Adapton Recipe
makes for it. Symbolic like space, with the intent explicit -- a time is a
name the program writes, not a counter the system hands out, which is what
lets a later run mean the same moment. And navigable: a program moves into a
time and can hold another as an ordinary value while it stands there.

  let t0 = Adapton.now(); do within time `t { (t0, Adapton.now()) }
    ==> (Now, Symbol("t"))

Outside, now() is the ambient present; inside, it is the symbol the program
named. Naming a time is then what makes a delayed put possible: the cell
reads Some(None) inside the block and Some(Some(1)) after it.

No chapter for deriveCompare. The attribute parses and the module loads, but
nothing implements it -- no comparison function is generated, so there is
nothing to run.

All eight evaluate with no errors, checked in the app rather than only
parsed.
