author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Add fumola_with: run a Fumola program on a Hazel value

The way in, wired up. The livelit carries a Hazel value in its model, renders
it into Fumola source, and binds it as `input` before the program runs, so
the program can name it -- and the result comes back translated as usual.

Built by extending MakeFumola rather than duplicating it: a takes_input flag
adds a fourth model component, typed Unknown because a model type is fixed
and the value a program runs on is whatever its author passes. The other two
livelits set it false and are unchanged, so all four share one path to the
runtime.

A value with no written Fumola form -- a hole, a function, a reference --
fails the expansion with the message saying what could not be written,
rather than running a program that does not mean what was written.

Two card cases: doubling 21 through "input + input", and the round trip that
matters, a Hazel list of symbol and number pairs leaving as [(`a, 1), (`b,
2)] and coming back with its symbols read as Symbol again. That is the shape
a sort over [(Symbol, Int)] needs.

The model test covers the four-part match specifically: nothing else
exercises it, and a model that fails to read back is silent -- the livelit
falls back to its default and the program loses what was written in it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Render Hazel values as Fumola source: the way in

Everything so far translates outward. This is the mirror: a Hazel value
becomes the text of a Fumola expression, so a program can be run *on*
something Hazel holds rather than only reporting back to it.

Source text rather than a marshalling format, for the same reason a thunk
name is source text: Fumola's own parser decides what its syntax means, and
Hazel needs to know none of it. The cost is that only values with a written
form can cross, which is every first-order value and nothing else.

Covers integers, booleans, floats, text, tuples, records, lists, options
(null and ?(x)), variant tags, and Hazel's Symbol type back into Fumola's
symbol syntax -- Name("x") as `x, Num(7) as 7, Call as `a(`b), Dot as `a.`b.
So the shape a sort wants, [(Symbol, Int)], renders as [(`b, 2), (`a, 1)].

Deliberately partial: a hole, a function or a reference into a runtime is
refused with a message naming what could not be written, never guessed at.

Known limit: symbol constructors are recognised by name, so a user's own
Name constructor in another type would render as a symbol. The
constructor's type is available once statics annotates it, which is where
that fix goes if a case needs it.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Cards: the event log as a table, and the first Fumola chapter

The adapton event log is a list of records, which is the shape a table
draws, so the card pins one: ^^probe_table(events) shows the log with a
column per field. Columns follow the order EventRow lists its fields, which
is why metaTime is written first.

^^probe_table, not ^^table -- a probe is a refractor and its trigger is
recognised in card text, where a projector invocation around a livelit is
not. Slides.re says as much in its header; it took a while to read.

Fumola / Gcd is the first chapter of what should become a series in
successive complexity, one per example in the Fumola repo. Gcd is the
smallest: a plain recursive function, called from Hazel, with nothing
incremental to reuse -- and, because a thunk is a value in Fumola and Hazel
has none of its own for one, a case showing a thunk beside its forced value.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Tables: read through an ascription, and fit a constructor in a cell

Two limits met while showing the adapton event log as a table.

parse_table matched a list literal directly, so an ascription around the
whole list was not peeled -- only rows were. An ascribed list is the
ordinary way to write a table whose element type a reader cannot infer, and
the only way to write one that comes from a livelit, since those expand only
in checking mode. It now normalises the list the same way it normalises a
row, reusing that helper.

max_column_length was 12, which fits a word or a number but not a
constructor with a payload: an adapton event reads
"AddNode(Symbol(\"g\"), Now, 1)", and every such cell came out as
"AddNode(...+3)", which says nothing. Raised to 32. Only cells longer than
the budget abbreviate, so names and numbers elsewhere are unaffected.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Show opaque Fumola values, and let the annotation order record fields

Two changes from reading the cards, both about what a value looks like when
it arrives.

A Fumola value Hazel cannot represent now arrives opaque, carrying the
source Fumola prints for it, and rides in the term a reference already uses
-- with no reference. An empty reads renders the description alone, so a
thunk in a tuple reads as "@thunk ({ Gcd.gcd(12, 18) })" rather than as a
red mark where a value belongs. It is a value: Hazel having no
representation for a thunk is a limit of the boundary, not an error in the
program. Only the reference case keeps the "peek(`x) = Some(41)" shape, and
only it needs the grouping parentheses.

Record fields now arrive in the order the expected type declares them.
Fumola holds them in a HashMap, so the runtime sorts by name to keep
successive evaluations from disagreeing -- but where a type is expected, its
author has already said what shape this is, including the order they want to
read it in. Name order still covers anything the annotation omits. Visible
immediately in a table, whose columns are the fields in order: writing
(metaTime=Int, event=Event) puts metaTime on the left.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Show what a cell holds when Hazel has no value for it

A reference to a cell holding a thunk showed "peek(`h) = ?". The hole was
honest and useless: something is in there, and the runtime can say what.

FumolaPeek gains a holds field carrying that description, so the reference
now shows

  peek(`h) = Some(@thunk ({ 1 + 3; pointer(`h) }))

the thunk's own source, printed by Fumola. Still Some, because the cell is
occupied; only a read with nothing to report shows a bare hole. The
self-referential case says so too, rather than holing out silently.

The description sits beside the value rather than in it, deliberately. The
value stays a hole, so a cell Hazel cannot represent reads as incomplete
rather than as an error -- putting the text in the value would have made it
an Invalid, and an annotation over it a type error.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Spell both of these Hazel's way: peek's option, and the mode

Two changes from reading the cards in the running app, both the same kind of
thing: a place where Fumola's spelling had leaked into an API Hazel users
read.

A reference showed as "peek(`x)! = 41". The `!` is Fumola's option-unwrap and
Hazel has no such operator, so the "! =" invites reading it as not-equals.
It now shows as

  peek(`x) = Some(41)

which is true of Fumola on its own terms -- peek answers an option -- and
spelled the way Hazel spells one. The evaluated program still carries the
`!`, since unwrapping is what lets a reference to a cell holding an Int be
used as an Int; the shown form and the run form are now separate, which is
safe because nothing re-evaluates the shown one. A read that found nothing
shows a bare hole rather than Some of one, which would claim more than is
known.

The fumola_new mode was a string holding one of two words. It is a choice
between named alternatives, so it is now a sum: Fumola writes
{#simple; #graphical} and Hazel writes + Simple + Graphical, so the livelit
takes ^fumola_new(7, Graphical). The runtime is still asked in Fumola's own
tags, which is the shim's business rather than the API's.

Also repairs two drifts in docs/livelits.md found on the way: the FumolaPeek
example still showed reads: "peek(1)!", and a stale section described a
pointer arriving as a ^fumola(...) livelit -- a form that has not existed
since there were three named ones.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Rename the fumola livelits, and add fumola_new

The names now say what the livelits are rather than how they were first
described. fumola_thunk becomes fumola_put_force, which is the Fumola
operation it performs: it puts a thunk in a named cell and forces it.
fumola_editor becomes fumola_eval, since "editor" names the mode it runs in
rather than what it does. "Instance" stays in prose and comments -- it is the
right word for an entry of sigma -- but is out of the livelit API. Nothing
depended on the old spellings: the design is new enough that no saved
programs carry them.

fumola_new is new. The other two livelits attach to whatever runtime their id
names, creating one with the default semantics if none exists, and nothing
said which semantics that should be -- every runtime got the same one by
uniformity rather than by anyone's decision, and once the mode is a choice
two ids could disagree. fumola_new is where a program decides, once, where
the runtime is made: ^fumola_new(7, "graphical") declares runtime 7 and
expands to 7, so every livelit sharing an id talks to a runtime whose mode
was declared.

Expanding to an Int is a compromise. The id wants to be abstract, hiding the
number, but Hazel's abstract types come only from polymorphic binders --
there is no signature sealing -- and a livelit cannot take a Hazel value as
an argument either, since expansion sees only the expected type and the type
tools, never the environment. So the handle is an Int by convention.

Declaring is idempotent in the runtime, which is what makes it safe to put in
a livelit at all: a livelit re-expands on every edit, and a reset would
discard the history the other livelits sharing that runtime have built.

The shim boundary moves out of MakeFumola so both it and fumola_new share one
copy. The card demonstrates the point: runtime 7 asks for graphical and can
report an event count, while runtime 0 -- everything else on the card --
stays simple, where there is no graph to count.

Kept as one commit because the rename spans code and cards together: a
commit renaming the cards without Livelit.re would fail its own doc-slide
test.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Card: name the two modes, and ask for peek in the right one

Fumola runs in two modes, and the two livelits are how a Hazel program picks
one, which the card never said.

A fumola_thunk encodes a forced thunk, forced by the editor: it names a
thunk, puts the program in it, and forces it. The program therefore runs on
a forceful stack, in the archivist mode, where the tracked operations belong
-- put (:=), get (@), and force. That is what the thunk name is for: the
name is the cell the thunk lives in, and the force is what a dependency can
be recorded against.

A fumola_editor runs its program on a force-free stack: the editor mode, the
more general one. reset and the graph introspection belong to it alone, and
a reset from inside a force refuses -- AdaptonError(UnreachableForceEnd),
which is what made this distinction visible.

peek is the interesting case, and the card had it wrong twice. It is how the
editor reads a cell, and it stays available inside a force as well, on
purpose: reading a cell without recording a dependency is how you look at a
computation while it runs. So a peek in a thunk is meaningful, merely
untracked. The two peek cases move to fumola_editor because that is where
the operation belongs, not because the alternative breaks.

Also adds the cases for the new translations: a float, a list, an empty
list, a list of tuples, and a record of floats shaped like Scene's Vec3.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Translate Fumola arrays as lists, and floats

A Fumola array is a purely functional sequence, and it has the same shape as
a Hazel list, so it crosses as one. The element type comes from the
annotation, the way a tuple's and a record's component types already do --
so a livelit checked against [Int] hands each element Int to translate
against, and an empty array is a list whose element type is simply left
open.

The Rust side already emitted "List" for Value::Array; nothing consumed it
here, so an array was untranslatable from Hazel's end alone. Adapton's own
introspection returns arrays -- peekEvents, and the edge lists inside
peekInfo -- so this is most of what that module reports.

Floats had no arm on either side. They arrive as text, like the integers, so
nothing passes through a JSON number on the way. The motivating case is
Adapton.Scene, whose Vec3 is three floats: no scene position could cross the
boundary without this.

body:
Flatten projectors on the path probes actually use

The previous commit fixed the wrong function. It flattened projectors in

which routes to simple_code -- and simple_code carries the same stated

should draw as a widget rather than as tokens.

evaluator strips a Projector, stepping to its body (Transition.re, kind

of evaluation, so a wrapper is gone by the time anyone could see it. That is
why the first attempt at this rendered as plain text.

rendered. Nothing carries it through evaluation, so there is nothing to
strip. The syntax underneath the projector is the old text form, so
unprojecting still reads.

values are built in language, which cannot look up into haz3lcore. The
projector draws from that model alone and consults neither statics nor the
syntax it wraps -- which is what lets it work in a result, rendered from a
bare segment with no info map behind it.

body:
Reintroduce the Symbol type, chosen by the expected type

A Fumola symbol now arrives either as structure or as its text, decided by
the type asked for:

    let s : String = ^fumola_thunk(..., "`hello")   ->  "hello"
    let s : Symbol = ^fumola_thunk(..., "`hello")   ->  Name("hello")

    type Symbol = + Num(Int) + Name(String)
                  + Call((Symbol, Symbol)) + Dot((Symbol, Symbol))

The type was added earlier and rolled back when the thunk livelit moved to
taking Fumola source for its name, which made a Hazel-side encoding
unnecessary for that purpose. It is wanted for the other direction: a symbol
coming out of a program is first-order data, and a Hazel program should be
able to take it apart rather than only read its text.

Both forms are kept because both earn their place. Structure is what you want
to inspect; text is the only way to produce a String from a livelit at all,
since a Hazel string literal cannot contain a quote and so neither can the
program that would otherwise build one. Nothing had to be chosen between them
because expansion is already type-directed -- the same mechanism that decides
which sum a variant belongs to decides this.

The structured form resolves its constructors through the ambient context
like any other variant, rather than inventing them, so it follows whichever
Symbol-shaped type is expected. Recursive through its own alias name, the way
type MyList = Nil + Cons(Int, MyList) is.

The documentation card gains both forms, the applied and numeric cases, and
sections on symbols in each direction: out of a program as values, and into
one as the name of a thunk.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Split the Fumola livelit into fumola_thunk and fumola_editor

The implicit thunk turned out to be the wrong thing to force on every
program. Wrapping as force(<name> := thunk { ... }) is what gives an edit its
incremental meaning, but it also puts the program inside a force, and some
things cannot run there: Adapton.reset() clears the store the enclosing force
is still inside, Adapton.peekForce asserts, and a binding made inside a thunk
does not outlive it.

So there are two, sharing one implementation:

- fumola_thunk wraps its program, and is what you want for a program whose
  value you are editing.
- fumola_editor evaluates at the top level. It is strictly more expressive --
  you can write the force(... := thunk { ... }) yourself -- and it is the only
  way to reach what the wrapper forbids.

Both name an instance, so two livelits carrying the same id share one runtime
and see each other's state and bindings: an editor can set up state that a
thunk reads.

Thunks are named after the livelit's own Hazel id rather than all being
`topLevel`, so two thunk livelits in one runtime keep separate histories
instead of overwriting each other. A Hazel id is a UUID, whose hyphens a
Fumola symbol cannot contain, so they are dropped and a letter prefixed.
Whether that id is stable across edits is not established here -- if it
changes, an edit starts a new thunk rather than reusing one, which costs
history rather than correctness.

A failed program now expands to a description of the failure, unless it
merely failed to parse. A half-written program is a syntax error on nearly
every keystroke and saying so would be noise; a program that parsed and then
went wrong is worth surfacing, and the expansion was the one place the reader
would otherwise see nothing.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Add FumolaPeek: a Fumola cell reference that carries its value

The first new exp_term form in this work -- everything until now was built
from existing ones. A Fumola pointer translates to it:

    1 := 2   ->   FumolaPeek({instance_id, reads: "peek(1)!", value: 2})

A value, not something that steps to one, so the reference stays visible in
the output rather than collapsing into the thing it refers to. Carrying the
result is what lets evaluation continue through it: a reference to a cell
holding an Int is usable as an Int. Before this the translated pointer was
inert -- ascribed Int but never producing one -- so a pair of pointers
typechecked as a pair of Ints and evaluated to a stuck pair.

Statics synthesizes the type of the carried value, so no annotation is
needed anywhere and the type is established rather than asserted. That also
removes the ascription and the separate type-synthesis pass: the value gives
the type.

Where a reference should behave as what it denotes, it does:

- Unboxing looks through, so a peek of a tuple still destructures.
- Equality compares the value denoted, so two peeks of different cells
  holding the same value are equal, while a reference stays equal to itself
  across a re-read.
- is_fun and match_exp recurse into the value.
- Substitution does not: the carried value is a translated Fumola result,
  and so is closed.

Rendering shows both halves, as `peek(1)! = 2`. There is no concrete syntax
for the form -- it is only ever produced by translation, never written or
parsed -- so this is a first cut rather than a settled choice, and changing
it touches only ExpToSegment.

A cell holding a pointer back to itself stops at a hole rather than being
followed forever, and an unreadable cell keeps its reference with an unknown
value.

The carried value is a snapshot, sound only because it is regenerated on
every expansion. It must never be persisted into a saved model, where it
would silently disagree with the runtime; this is noted on the form itself.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Read a pointer with peek, not get

Translating a result should not change the runtime being translated. get
records a dependency in the adapton graph, and translation runs on every
statics pass, so a dependency-recording read grew the graph as a side effect
of merely looking at a value.

The generated livelit reads the same way, so what it runs matches what typed
it:

    1 := 2   ->   (^fumola(<same id>, "peek(1)!") : Int)

The `!` unwraps peek's option, assuming the cell is defined. It is in the
case that matters, since the pointer came from a value the runtime just
produced. A pointer to a cell that has since gone away now reads as an error

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Type a translated pointer by dereferencing it

A pointer is now translated as the livelit that reads it, ascribed with the
type of what it actually points at:

    1 := 2   ->   (^fumola(<same id>, "get(1)") : Int)

The type comes from the runtime rather than from anything Hazel could have
known: translation runs get(<name>) in the same instance and takes the type
of the answer. A pointer to a pointer is typed by following the whole chain.

This also fixes an error I introduced an hour ago and did not anticipate.
The generated livelit carried no annotation, while the fumola livelit had
just been made to require one, so every pointer result asked for an
annotation that nobody could write -- it is code the user never typed.
Dereferencing supplies it honestly.

Details worth knowing:

- Cycles terminate. A cell holding a pointer back to itself would otherwise
  dereference forever, so the pointers already followed on a path are
  tracked and a repeat yields Unknown.

- Anything unresolvable -- an unreadable cell, a variant whose home type
  cannot be recovered, a translation failure -- becomes Unknown, which is
  always a sound ascription.

- An option is ascribed Hazel's own Option rather than a synthesized
  one-variant sum, which would typecheck here and fail to interoperate
  anywhere else.

- Dereferencing goes through a new uncached shim entry point. These calls
  must not be cached, since a later edit can change what a cell holds, and
  they must not evict the cached main program either -- the cache holds only
  the last program per instance, so alternating between the two would make
  every render re-run everything.

Note that dereferencing uses get, which records a dependency in the adapton
graph. Translation therefore has an effect on the runtime it is inspecting.
peek would avoid that; get is what was asked for, and is what the generated
livelit itself will run.

Hazel-side only -- the AdaptonPointer tag already carries the text.

body:

convention holds throughout: `adapton(`settings) renders as
"adapton(settings)".

This also answers a limitation we kept running into. Hazel string literals
admit no escapes -- Token.is_string permits at most two quote characters in a
token -- so a livelit's program can never contain a double quote, and there
was no way to produce a string from a livelit at all. Naming a symbol
produces the text instead.

`adapton(`settings) as Symbol/Call, and that symbols inside tuples translate
like any other component. Two things I could not exercise from surface
syntax: `a.`b is a syntax error in Fumola, so the Dot case is written to the
JSON shape but never seen from a real program; and a bare 7 evaluates to an
Int rather than a symbol, since numbers act as symbols only in name position.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Expand the fumola livelit in checking mode, directed by the expected type

A Fumola variant carries no home type. Fumola tags live in one flat
namespace: #Bar(3) is a value whether or not anyone declared Bar. Hazel
constructors are the opposite -- Bar means the Bar of some sum type in scope,
and typing it needs that type. So the boundary was lossy in exactly the
direction that matters, and every Fumola variant arrived as a free
constructor, unfixable from the program text because statics splices a
livelit's expansion in already-elaborated and never traverses it.

Expansion is now type-directed. expand receives the type expected of it and
pushes that expectation down through tuples, records, options and variants,
resolving each tag against the type actually asked for.

Consequences worth noting:

- The fumola livelit requires checking mode. Its result shape depends on both
  the program it runs and the type asked of it, so with no expected type it
  says so -- a new LivelitNeedsAnnotation mark -- rather than guessing. This
  replaces the earlier expedient of declaring its expansion type Unknown,
  which asserted a type rather than establishing one.

- Option stops being special-cased. None and Some previously carried
  hard-coded BuiltinsADT.Option annotations because that was the one type I
  knew statically; they now resolve through the same path as any other
  constructor, against whatever Option-shaped type is expected.

- A name that resolves to nothing is left unannotated rather than guessed at,
  so Hazel marks it free. That is the honest outcome: the name belongs to no
  sum type in scope.

expand takes closures rather than a Ctx.t, because Ctx already depends on
LivelitCtx -- Ctx.entry has a LivelitEntry of raw_livelit -- so naming Ctx.t
in the livelit interface would be circular. It is also the tighter interface:
a livelit needs to resolve names and unfold aliases, not read the context.

The other three livelits ignore the new arguments and set
requires_annotation = false.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Translate Fumola's option into Hazel's

type in BuiltinsADT.

The constructors carry the same type annotations BuiltinsADT.Option gives
them, so they elaborate the way a hand-written None or Some(x) would, and
they are rebuilt on each call rather than reusing the values in BuiltinsADT,
which would share one id across every occurrence.

No Fumola-side change was needed: the runtime already emitted Null and
Option, added when peek(s) was introduced. Until now Hazel had nowhere to
put them, so peek reported that it could not translate a Null. It now reads
as None for a name that was never written and Some(v) for one that was.

peek(hit) and peek(miss) all produce the shapes these tests assume.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Translate Fumola tuples, records and variants into Hazel values

reading two cells back as (get(1), get(2)) gives an actual Hazel pair rather
than something a program has to take apart.

The expansion type becomes Unknown. A Fumola result has no single static
type -- 1 + 2 is an Int while (get(1), get(2)) is a pair -- so no fixed type
is right for every program. Hazel's gradual typing lets a livelit be used
wherever its actual result fits, and mismatches surface as ordinary type
errors. The alternative, a FumolaValue sum type, would be statically honest
but would hand back a wrapper rather than a pair, which defeats the purpose.

The shim now passes the runtime's JSON through verbatim. The previous tagged
string ("Int:3") could not carry structure.

Translation lives in FumolaValue rather than inside Livelit.Fumola so it can
be tested directly: the livelit itself can only be exercised in a browser
with the wasm runtime loaded, which left the step that actually builds Hazel
values unverified. Test_FumolaValue covers it, including the pair case,

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Keep the livelit on one runtime across edits

State written to a pointer in one edit was not visible to the next, which
defeats the point of the whole thing. The runtime was never at fault: at the
shim level, "1 := 2" followed by a separate eval of
@(prim "adaptonPointer" (1)) returns 2, both in the browser and in the REPL.
Hazel was moving the livelit onto a different runtime between edits.

Three causes, all in this layer:

- The view observed the instance it had just claimed while expand observed
  the instance the model names. Those can differ, so the widget could show a
  result computed in a different runtime from the one the program evaluates
  in. Both now read the model, and a claim takes effect from the next render.

- A claim is only settled once the model has been rewritten to name the new
  runtime. Until that lands the livelit still reads as id 0 and claims again,
  which allocated a fresh runtime every render. Claims are now idempotent per
  owner.

- The wasm was loaded with a bare relative specifier from inside code built
  by `new Function`, which has no active script, so the specifier did not
  reliably resolve against the page: served from one port it tried to fetch
  the runtime from another. Both URLs are now resolved against document.baseURI.

Rebuilds the wasm so it carries the symbol translation. A value like "1 := 2"
evaluates to something that coerces to a symbol, so it now reports that the
livelit cannot render a Symbol as an Int, rather than the misleading "no
Hazel translation". Reading an Int back out is unaffected.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Fix a crash on clicking a livelit, and stop rendering from rewriting syntax

Two bugs, one pre-existing and one mine.

Clicking any livelit projector whose view could not find a model crashed
with an assertion failure from JsUtil.get_elem_by_id. The projector attaches
its id only in the branch where get_model succeeds; the "No livelit found"
fallback is a bare text node with no id, so the focus handler asserted on a
missing element. This affects slider and emotion on dev too -- both livelits
in the Documentation slide render that fallback. focus_pointer now treats a
missing element as nothing to focus.

Separately, the fumola livelit re-claimed its instance on every render so
that a duplicated livelit could be given a fresh runtime. That makes
rendering rewrite the syntax being rendered: a projector's id is the id of
its syntax root, so the rewrite can change the owner, invalidating the next
claim and rewriting again. It now claims only from instance id 0, which
cannot loop.

The cost is that a copied livelit inherits its original's id and so shares
its execution history. That is a real gap, and it needs a projector identity
that survives a model edit; the previous code assumed info.id was such an
identity without establishing it.

Also passes the wasm init argument as an object, quieting a deprecation
warning on every page load.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Add a Fumola livelit backed by external incremental runtime state

An MVP for running Fumola programs inside Hazel. Unlike the existing
livelits, this one's model does not contain all of its own state: it holds
a pair

    (instance_id, program_text)

where instance_id names an entry of an external store

    sigma : FumolaInstanceId -> FumolaRuntimeState

held by the Fumola wasm module and reached through the window.fumola shim
in prebundle.js. The Fumola interpreter and its Adapton demanded
computation graph are deliberately not serialized into the Hazel model;
only the name is.

Three things follow, and each had to be done explicitly:

- Editing preserves the id, so the edit re-evaluates against the same live
  runtime instead of starting over.
- Expansion is an observation of sigma, not stored state. The result is
  never a second source of truth in the model.
- Ids are generative. Duplicating a livelit must not give two widgets one
  shared execution history, so the view claims its instance using the
  projector's persistent identity and takes a fresh runtime when another
  live projector already owns the id it names. The same mechanism realizes
  a runtime on reload, when a saved program names an id the session has
  never seen.

To support that last point, the livelit view now receives the projector's
id. Existing livelits ignore it.

The wasm runtime is built by scripts/build-fumola-wasm.sh against the
fumola_wasm crate in the Fumola repo. The generated .js and .wasm are
committed because branch previews deploy src/web/www verbatim; without them
the preview would have no runtime. Hazel still builds when they are absent,
and the livelit degrades to a message rather than breaking evaluation.

Not settled here: FumolaInstanceId is an ordinary Int in the model rather
than a distinct opaque value form, only first-order integer results are
translated, and Fumola values whose meaning depends on the runtime have no
Hazel representation.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Add a settings axis and separate fairness from extrapolation

A colleague raised that benchmarking headless Hazel may mislead, since much
of what makes Hazel slow is the information statics and evaluation record
for the UI. Two distinct questions were tangled in that, and they need
different answers.

Fairness between backends was already satisfied and is now stated: one
source tree, one settings record, one switch, one compiler version, only the
backend flag differs, and matching result checksums confirm both sides
compute the same answer.

Extrapolation to app-level speedup is not satisfied and cannot be by this
harness. To probe the gap rather than assume it away, evaluation now runs
under both probe_all=false and probe_all=true -- probe_all is off even in
CoreSettings.on, so the previous numbers measured a leaner path than the
editor runs. The two profiles are indistinguishable on these workloads.

Statics is also sampled, but only cold: Statics.mk is memoized, so a loop
measures cache hits. The single-shot sample is dominated by JIT warm-up (the
same program timed 16.6 ms and 3.2 ms in different profiles) and is labelled
as unusable for conclusions.

The workloads are compute-heavy programs that are textually tiny, the
opposite shape from the editor. That is why evaluation dominates statics
here, and why the result is 'the evaluator is ~3.5x faster', not 'Hazel is'.

author: Matthew Hammer
body:
Fixed-precision workloads: wasm_of_ocaml is ~4x faster

Leaning on Hazel's fixed-precision types sidesteps the bignum wall. SInt
(machine int) and Float avoid Bigint entirely, so bench/fixed-*.hz uses only
those, and BigIntWasmStub swaps bignum out of the build.

Getting bignum out cascaded further than expected. Statics.re had exactly one
use of Jane Street Core (Core.Memo.general); replacing it with Util.Memo
removed Core from the evaluator's cone entirely. Sets, AST, Parser.mly and
Lexer.mll reached the bignum package directly and now go through util's
BigInt wrapper, which is portable across both builds.

The stub keeps construction and comparison total, because Builtins.ctx_init
needs them to boot, and makes arithmetic raise: a workload reaching Int or
Nat fails loudly rather than silently benchmarking 63-bit math.

Results, both backends from js_of_ocaml 6.2.0 on node 22, 20 iterations,
with matching result checksums across backends:

  sint-fib        1050 ms -> 285 ms   3.7x
  float-numeric    290 ms ->  74 ms   3.9x
  sint-list        168 ms ->  42 ms   4.0x

Between-workload differences are inside the noise -- the ordering flipped
across two runs -- so only the ~4x headline is claimed.

Also corrects a note in passing: the evaluator is explicitly trampolined
(Trampoline.re), and both tail and non-tail Hazel recursion reach depth
20000+ under js_of_ocaml. Deep recursion is not a backend risk.

Verified: dune build src bench --profile release clean, @test-quick 3457
tests passing.

body:
SPIKE: Bonsai-free evaluator benchmark for wasm_of_ocaml

virtual_dom v0.16 requires js_of_ocaml < 6.0.0 and wasm_of_ocaml is only
released from 6.0.1, so the two cannot coexist in one opam switch. Anything
in the Bonsai cone therefore cannot be compiled to Wasm at all, and making
[language] Bonsai-free is a precondition for measuring the evaluator.

(Bonsai/Virtual_dom). Util_web re-exports all of Util, so most consumers
only changed `open Util` to `open Util_web`. JsUtil and Key were each split
rather than moved, keeping their js_of_ocaml-only majority in [util]; that
alone avoided ~48 files of churn.

Virtual_dom, since the three builtin livelits construct vdom directly.
LivelitCtx keeps its types so Ctx.LivelitEntry still typechecks, but nothing
populates it and LivelitProj renders a placeholder. This part is NOT
mergeable -- the principled version registers livelit views from the web
layer.

Add bench/wasm, which links only [language] + [menhirParser] and parses via
menhirParser rather than the haz3lcore zipper path. It emits the JSON shape
bench/compare.js already consumes. setup-switch.sh builds the Bonsai-free
switch; run.sh builds both backends from the same compiler version and runs
